title: Greece Approves €3.5B Israeli "Achilles Shield" — Anti-Missile System Amid PM's Turkey "Threat of War" Warning
excerpt: Greece's KYSEA approved a €3.5B 'Achilles Shield' air defense system from Israel — Rafael, IAI, David's Sling — as PM Mitsotakis warns of Turkey's 'open threat of war.' What's inside the deal?
content:
Greece approved the purchase of a €3.5 billion air defense system from Israel on Thursday, giving the green light to a program the country is calling "Achilles Shield."

The decision was made by KYSEA — Greece's national security council — which formally approved the procurement contracts. The system, worth up to €3.5 billion (approximately $4 billion), is built around technology from two Israeli defense companies: Rafael and IAI. The program incorporates Rafael's Spyder surface-to-air missile system, IAI's Barak MX missile defense system, and the David's Sling interceptor — all integrated under a single unified command network. Greek companies will participate in 25% of the project.

KYSEA also approved several additional purchases in the same session: three Embraer C-390 military transport aircraft from Brazil, ten British-built VICTA mini-submarines designed for special operations, American V-BAT unmanned aerial vehicles, and Heron reconnaissance drones from Israel.

The "Achilles Shield" is designed to handle threats across three different layers — ballistic missiles, aircraft, and drones — simultaneously. The three Israeli systems together cover that full range, from short-range drone intercepts to medium and long-range missile threats.

The approvals are part of a much larger Greek military modernization plan. Greece has committed to spending around €28 billion on defense by 2036 — a program that also includes plans for up to 40 F-35 fighter jets from the United States and additional frigates from France and Italy.

Greece spends approximately 3.5% of its gross domestic product on defense — a proportion higher than most NATO members. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis described what he called an "open threat of war" from neighboring Turkey during a NATO summit in Ankara earlier this month.

Greece and Israel already have an established military partnership, operating a joint air training center on Greek soil and conducting annual joint exercises. They also cooperate on anti-drone technology and cybersecurity.

For Greece, the Achilles Shield represents years of planning made formal. For Israel's defense industry, it is one of the largest export deals in its history.
